section.title: The Second Journey: Corinth
section.sectionRationale: In Corinth, a wealthy and immoral commercial hub, Paul settles for a year and a half, working as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla and testifying that Jesus is the Christ. When opposition mounts, the Lord Himself speaks in a vision, promising protection and a people already His in that city. Gallio's refusal to hear the case against Paul shields the mission, and Paul returns at last to Antioch, closing the second journey.
section.thesis: The risen Christ sustains His discouraged servant and guards His mission in a hostile city, assuring Paul that He already has a people there, so that the gospel takes deep root in Corinth under God's providential protection even from a Roman proconsul.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Paul's arrival, tentmaking, and preaching in Corinth; the Lord's night vision of encouragement and the year and a half of teaching; the hearing before Gallio and his dismissal of the charges; and Paul's departure, his vow, and his return through Ephesus to Antioch.

units.label: Paul ministers in Corinth
units.note: tentmaking, reasoning, and turning to the Gentiles

verses.text: After this, Paul left Athens and went to Corinth.
There he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to visit them,
and he stayed and worked with them because they were tentmakers by trade, just as he was.
Every Sabbath he {{dialegomai|reasoned}} in the synagogue, trying to {{peitho|persuade}} Jews and Greeks alike.
And when Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself fully to the word, testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the {{christos|Christ}}.
But when they opposed and insulted him, he shook out his garments and told them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent of it. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.”
So Paul left the synagogue and went next door to the house of Titus Justus, a worshiper of God.
Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his whole household believed in the Lord. And many of the Corinthians who heard the message believed and were baptized.

units.label: The Lord's encouragement
units.note: I have many people in this city

verses.text: One night the Lord spoke to Paul in a vision: “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking; do not be silent.
For I am with you and no one will lay a hand on you, because I have many {{laos|people}} in this city.”
So Paul stayed for a year and a half, teaching the word of God among the Corinthians.
While Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews coordinated an attack on Paul and brought him before the judgment seat.
“This man is persuading the people to worship God in ways contrary to the law,” they said.
But just as Paul was about to speak, Gallio told the Jews, “If this matter involved a wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, it would be reasonable for me to hear your complaint.
But since it is a dispute about words and names and your own law, settle it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of such things.”
And he drove them away from the judgment seat.
At this, the crowd seized Sosthenes the synagogue leader and beat him in front of the judgment seat. But none of this was of concern to Gallio.

units.label: Paul returns to Antioch
units.note: a vow, a promise to return, and the journey home

verses.text: Paul remained in Corinth for quite some time before saying goodbye to the brothers. He had his head shaved in Cenchrea to keep a vow he had made, and then he sailed for Syria, accompanied by Priscilla and Aquila.
When they reached Ephesus, Paul left Priscilla and Aquila. He himself went into the synagogue there and reasoned with the Jews.
When they asked him to stay for a while longer, he declined.
But as he left, he said, “I will come back to you if God is willing.” And he set sail from Ephesus.
When Paul had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church at Jerusalem. Then he went down to Antioch.

dialegomai.gloss: To reason, discuss, argue a case back and forth; the root of the English dialogue. Luke often uses it of Paul's synagogue ministry. Preaching the gospel is not bare assertion; Paul lays out the Scriptures and reasons toward the conclusion that Jesus is the Christ.

peitho.gloss: To persuade, to win over, to bring to conviction. Paul aims not merely to inform but to persuade Jews and Greeks. Persuasion honours the hearer's mind, yet Acts makes clear that only the Lord opens hearts to be truly persuaded of the gospel.

christos.gloss: Christ, the Anointed One, the Greek for the Hebrew Messiah. Paul's whole testimony in the synagogue presses one point: that Jesus is the Christ, the promised anointed King of Israel. This is the fault line that both gathers believers and provokes opposition.

laos.gloss: A people, especially a people belonging to God. The Lord tells Paul He has many laos in Corinth, people not yet converted but already His by election. The word once reserved for Israel now embraces those God will call to Himself in a pagan city, grounding evangelism in God's prior choice.

basic.context: Paul arrives in Corinth, a rich, rough port city, and settles in for the longest stay of the journey. He supports himself as a tentmaker alongside Aquila and Priscilla, reasons weekly in the synagogue, and, when opposed, turns to the Gentiles. Discouragement seems near, so the Lord speaks to him in a vision. Later the proconsul Gallio refuses to hear the charges against him, and Paul finally returns to Antioch.
basic.hermeneutics: The heart of the passage is the night vision. The key question is what keeps a servant of God going in a hard place. The answer is not results alone but a word from the Lord: do not be afraid, keep speaking, I am with you, and I have many people in this city. Read the whole account in the light of that promise and God's providence through Gallio.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul dialegomai, reasons, in the synagogue and seeks to peitho, persuade, Jews and Greeks that Jesus is the christos, the Messiah. The turning point is God's word that He has many laos, people, in Corinth, a people already His by election, waiting to be called through the preached word.
basic.typology: Paul's vow and shaved head at Cenchrea recall the Nazirite devotion of the Old Testament, a life set apart to God. The Lord's promise, I am with you, echoes His words to Moses, Joshua, and the prophets, now spoken to His apostle as he carries the gospel to the nations.
basic.christ: The risen Christ is present and active. It is He who appears to Paul in the vision, He whom Paul preaches as the Christ, and He who claims a people in Corinth as His own. His presence, not the mood of the city, is Paul's confidence.
basic.god: God is sovereign and faithful. He has a chosen people even in immoral Corinth, He promises His presence and protection, and He restrains opposition through a Roman proconsul who unwittingly serves the mission. Election does not silence evangelism; it fuels it.
basic.crossReferences: The Corinthian letters flow from this ministry. 2 Timothy shows Paul's tentmaking companions and his hardship. The promise I am with you echoes Isaiah 41 and Matthew 28. Romans 8 grounds evangelism in God's foreknown and called people.
basic.oneStory: The gospel plants deep roots in one of the great cities of the empire. The one story of Scripture, God calling out a people for His name, advances as the risen Christ assures Paul of a people already His in Corinth and guards the mission until the word takes hold.

context.literary:
Luke handles Corinth with a lightness that hides its design. The section divides cleanly into four panels: Paul at work and in the synagogue, verses 1 to 8; the Lord's night word, verses 9 and 10, with the summary of a year and a half in verse 11; the hearing before Gallio, verses 12 to 17; and the voyage home, verses 18 to 22. The vision sits in the middle, and the layout makes it the pivot. What comes before it is pressure, expulsion and fear. What follows is proof that the promise held: nobody lays a hand on Paul, and the proconsul himself dismisses the case.

The passage turns on a repeated pattern of rejection and turning. Paul reasons in the synagogue, is opposed, and goes to the Gentiles, verse 6. Luke has told this story twice before, at Pisidian Antioch, 13:46, and he will tell it a final time in Rome, 28:28. Each time the turn is real, and each time it is not final, since Paul is back in a synagogue at Ephesus within a few verses, 18:19. The pattern is not a once-for-all verdict but a rhythm: to the Jew first, then to the Gentile, as Romans 1:16 says.

Luke uses names to build a community. Aquila and Priscilla, Titus Justus, Crispus and Sosthenes appear without ceremony. Aquila and Priscilla frame the whole section, since they appear in verse 2 and are still with Paul when he leaves, verse 18. Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believes in verse 8; Sosthenes, who is also called a synagogue ruler, is beaten in verse 17. The reader senses a real city with real faces.

One more detail is worth noting. In verse 12 the Jews 'coordinated' their attack, which in Greek means they rose up with one accord. That is the word for the unity of the first believers in Acts 1:14 and 2:46. Opposition can be as united as worship.
context.historical:
Corinth was a Roman colony, rebuilt by Julius Caesar in 44 BC, and by Paul's day the capital of the province of Achaia and a wealthy trading city. It sat astride the narrow isthmus with a harbour on either side, Lechaeum to the west and Cenchreae to the east, so goods and travellers passed through constantly. The Isthmian Games were held nearby, and visitors came in numbers. The city had a reputation for loose living, and Paul's later letters to the church there deal with divisions, lawsuits, sexual immorality and abuse of the Lord's Supper.

Tentmaking was a respectable trade, and it fitted a world of travellers, soldiers and festival crowds who needed shelter. Teachers in the Greek world often took payment from students, and wandering philosophers might depend on patrons. Paul chose to support himself by his own hands. He tells the Thessalonians that he did so to avoid burdening them, 1 Thessalonians 2:9, and he tells the Corinthians that he did not use his right to be paid, 1 Corinthians 9:12 and 2 Corinthians 11:7-9. The arrival of Silas and Timothy in verse 5, who brought help from Macedonia, 2 Corinthians 11:9, probably relieved him of full time labour, which would explain why he could then devote himself fully to preaching.

The edict of Claudius that expelled Jews from Rome is dated by many to about AD 49. The Roman writer Suetonius speaks of disturbances among the Jews at the instigation of someone named Chrestus, which some link to disputes over Christ. That would mean Aquila and Priscilla were probably refugees from a dispute that already involved the gospel.

Gallio's term can be dated with unusual precision. An inscription at Delphi mentions him as proconsul of Achaia, which places him around AD 51 to 52 and gives scholars a fixed point for the whole chronology of Paul's life. Gallio, brother of the philosopher Seneca, heard the case at the judgment seat, the bema, which stood in the public square of Corinth. His refusal to rule effectively treated the church as a branch of Judaism within Roman law, a protection that lasted for a time.
context.canonical:
The Corinth section draws on Old Testament patterns of calling and commission and then connects directly to the letters written from and to this city.

The Lord's words in the vision belong to a family of speeches. 'Do not be afraid' and 'I am with you' are the formula of Genesis 26:24, of Joshua 1:9, of Isaiah 41:10 and 43:5, and of Jeremiah 1:8, where the Lord tells the young prophet not to fear them, for He is with him. The Lord addresses Paul as He addressed the prophets. The statement that He has many people in the city calls to mind God's answer to Elijah that He had kept seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal, 1 Kings 19:18, which Paul himself cites in Romans 11:2-5.

Paul's words in verse 6, 'Your blood be on your own heads,' echo the watchman of Ezekiel, who is free of guilt if he gives warning and the people do not heed, Ezekiel 33:1-9. Paul uses the same image at Ephesus, Acts 20:26-27, and Ezekiel 3:18-19 supplies the background. The turn to the Gentiles echoes the servant's call to be a light to the nations, Isaiah 49:6, as Paul had said at Pisidian Antioch, 13:47.

The letters bring the story to life. The first and second letters to the Thessalonians were most likely written from Corinth in this period. Paul's letters to the Corinthians mention people from this chapter: Crispus and Gaius were among the few he baptised, 1 Corinthians 1:14, and he reminds them that he came to them in weakness, fear and much trembling, 1 Corinthians 2:3, which is the fear the Lord answers in the vision. Aquila and Priscilla appear again, with a church in their house, in Romans 16:3-5 and 1 Corinthians 16:19. Paul's promise to return if the Lord wills is the same attitude James teaches, James 4:13-15, and Paul himself repeats it in 1 Corinthians 4:19.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wanted his readers to see that God does not abandon His servants when they are afraid. He places the vision at a low point, after rejection by the synagogue and, as Paul later says, in weakness and fear, and he shows that the Lord's word is enough. It is no accident that the longest stay of the journey follows directly on the night word.

He also wanted readers to see how the Lord uses civil authority. Gallio is no friend of the church and no enemy. He is a Roman official who refuses to be drawn into a religious dispute, and by refusing he protects the mission. Luke's readers, many of whom might one day stand before magistrates, learn that the courts are neither always hostile nor always friendly, and that God works through both.

Luke wanted to display the humble life of the apostle: working with his hands beside two refugees, living next door to the synagogue and eventually taking a Gentile's house for his base. The mission is not run from a seat of power. And he wanted to show that the church grows from households and from a community of ordinary workers, many of whose names the letters preserve.

Finally the section tells how the second journey ends. Paul returns, greets the church and goes home to Antioch, which is where he had been sent out, so that the report of what God did can be given to those who sent him.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The vision is told as something that happened to Paul on a particular night. The passage does not promise every discouraged believer a vision, nor does it promise that no one will ever be harmed. 'No one will lay a hand on you' was a promise for this city and this work, and Paul's later life includes beatings and prison. What does carry across is the character of the God who speaks: He knows His servants' fear, He is with them, and He has people He intends to gather.

Paul's turning to the Gentiles is descriptive of what happened in Corinth, not a command to abandon any group. He goes back to the synagogue in Ephesus almost at once, and in Romans 9 to 11 he grieves for his own people. It would misread the passage to take it as permission to write anyone off.

The vow at Cenchrea is recorded without comment, and Luke does not tell believers to take such vows. Paul's later principle in 1 Corinthians 9:20 is that he became as a Jew to win Jews. The prescriptive core is what the Lord says to Paul and, by extension, to all who speak of Him: do not be afraid, keep on speaking, do not be silent. Tentmaking is also descriptive, but it shows a model of a worker who accepts the burden himself so that the gospel is not hindered.

debates.question: Does 'I have many people in this city' teach that God has already chosen certain Corinthians?

views.label: Yes, unconditional election
views.case: The Lord says it before most of them have heard the gospel. The word for people, laos, is the word used of God's own people, and Luke elsewhere says that those 'appointed for eternal life' believed, Acts 13:48. On this view the verse shows that God's choice stands behind and gives success to the preaching, John 10:16.

views.label: A promise of fruitfulness grounded in foreknowledge
views.case: Others say the statement fits the idea that God knew who would respond. They point out that the promise does not say how He chose them and that elsewhere Scripture calls on all people to repent, Acts 17:30.

views.label: A promise about the harvest, not a doctrine of the decree
views.case: A third group emphasises that the purpose of the verse is encouragement. The Lord is not answering a question about why some believe and others do not but telling a frightened worker that his work will not be in vain.

debates.bearing: All three views agree on what Paul does: he stays eighteen months and keeps teaching. The verse is meant to fuel mission, not to replace it, and it shows that God's sovereignty works through human preaching rather than apart from it.

debates.question: Were Aquila and Priscilla already believers when Paul met them?

views.label: Yes, they were Christians from Rome
views.case: Luke calls Aquila a Jew but says nothing about their conversion and makes no mention of Paul baptising them. A church existed in Rome before Paul arrived, and the edict possibly arose from disputes about Christ, so it is natural that they arrived as believers. They later teach Apollos, 18:26, which suggests maturity.

views.label: They became Christians through Paul
views.case: Others say that Paul's staying and working with them for so long, and Paul's later calling them fellow workers, fit a conversion in Corinth. The silence of Luke is not proof either way.

debates.bearing: The text leaves it open, and Luke's interest lies in their partnership. Whichever view is held, they become some of Paul's closest friends, risking their necks for his life, Romans 16:3-4.

debates.question: Whose vow was it, and what kind of vow?

views.label: Paul's Nazirite-style vow
views.case: Most readers take Paul as the one who shaved his head, in thanksgiving or in prayer during the Corinthian stay. Numbers 6:1-21 describes the Nazirite vow, and Paul later joins others in vows at Jerusalem, Acts 21:23-26. His readiness shows he was still observing the customs of his people.

views.label: Aquila's vow
views.case: The Greek participle for shaving could refer to either man, and Aquila is the nearer name. Those who hold this view say that nothing else in the story suggests Paul had made such a vow.

views.label: A different kind of vow
views.case: Since the Nazirite's hair was normally cut at the temple, Numbers 6:18, some say a vow made abroad was of a related but less formal kind, a vow of thanks or dedication.

debates.bearing: The details are unclear, and Luke gives no moral. What is clear is that Paul has not rejected his Jewish heritage, which is a fair reminder that turning to the Gentiles in Corinth did not mean turning from Jewish piety.

study.originalLanguages:
Luke's vocabulary in this section moves between the workshop, the synagogue and the court, and several words carry more than English shows.

Tentmakers in verse 3 translates skenopoios, a word that probably covers working in leather or goat hair cloth as well as making tents. In a city of travellers the work was steady. The related noun skene is the word for the tabernacle, tent of meeting, in the Greek Old Testament, and the shared root is a quiet reminder that Paul works with his hands in the shadow of a larger tent.

In verse 5 Paul 'devoted himself fully to the word.' The verb is synecho, to hold together, to press or constrain, and in the passive it can mean to be gripped or absorbed by something. It describes a man held by his message. Some ancient manuscripts have 'the Spirit' in place of 'the word,' but the sense of a man gripped by his message is clear either way.

The opposition in verse 6 is described by two verbs, antitassomai, to range oneself against, as an army arrays itself, and blasphemeo, to speak abusively, which is the word for blasphemy. The charge touches the holiest things. Paul answers with a gesture, shaking out his garments, which is the cousin of shaking dust off the feet in Acts 13:51 and Nehemiah's shaking out of his lap in Nehemiah 5:13, a symbolic act that declares he has done what he can.

In verse 9 the Lord says, 'Do not be afraid, keep on speaking, do not be silent.' The two positive commands are in the present tense, speak continually, and the negative command with a present tense fits a fear that had been going on. It matches what Paul later recalls of his state, weakness, fear and much trembling, 1 Corinthians 2:3. The promise that no one will lay a hand on him is followed in the Greek by the phrase 'to harm you,' kakoo, which clarifies that the promise is about protection from injury, not from every touch of suffering.

Paul 'stayed' a year and a half in verse 11, and the verb is kathizo, which in the active means to sit or settle. It is the posture of a teacher. Luke gives the length as a year and six months, a rare precision.

In verse 15 Gallio calls the dispute a matter of 'words and names and your own law,' logos, onomata and nomos. His list unwittingly names the three things at stake: the message, the person of Jesus as Christ, and the Law. His refusal, 'I refuse to be a judge of such things,' is a judicial decision that treats the matter as internal to Judaism.

The final word to note is in verse 21: 'if God is willing,' literally God willing. It is the stance of the creature before the Creator, and James 4:15 gives the same advice.

typology.type: The seven thousand and the many people, 1 Kings 19:18
typology.fulfillment: Elijah, exhausted and afraid, believed he was the only faithful one left, and the Lord answered that He had kept seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal. Paul, afraid and opposed, is told that the Lord has many people in this city. The correspondence is a discouraged servant corrected by the secret work of God. In Christ the reserved remnant is no longer one nation's faithful few but people gathered from every nation, as Romans 11:4-5 reads the Elijah story as a pattern of grace. The type falls short because Elijah's remnant was found within Israel, whereas Corinth's people were pagans, many of them from lives marked out in 1 Corinthians 6:9-11.

typology.type: The watchman and the blood, Ezekiel 33
typology.fulfillment: The watchman who blows the trumpet and is not heard is free from the blood of the people, and the one who fails to warn is guilty. Paul's words in verse 6 take the role of this watchman and are repeated at Ephesus, Acts 20:26-27. The correspondence is that a messenger is accountable for faithful warning, not for the response. In Christ the watchman role is carried by all who proclaim the gospel, and Christ Himself is the one who has warned and wept over Jerusalem, Luke 13:34. The type falls short because the watchman only warns of a coming sword, while the gospel offers a rescue.

typology.type: The judgment seat of Gallio and the judgment seat of Christ
typology.fulfillment: At the bema in Corinth a human judge declines to judge and sends the case away. Paul later tells these same Corinthians that all will stand before the judgment seat of Christ, 2 Corinthians 5:10, and the Romans that all will stand before God's, Romans 14:10. The correspondence is the same word, bema, and the same place of decision. The contrast is that Gallio refuses to judge while Christ will judge with justice, Acts 17:31, and none of that will be dismissed. The type is a contrast rather than a prophecy.

typology.type: A light to the nations, Isaiah 49:6
typology.fulfillment: The servant of the Lord is told that restoring Israel is too small a task, and that He will be a light for the Gentiles so salvation reaches the ends of the earth. Paul quoted this at Pisidian Antioch, Acts 13:47, and his turn in Corinth, verse 6, acts on it. Christ is the light of the world, John 8:12, and His body carries the light. The pattern falls short because the servant's work is finished by Christ alone, and the apostles only bear witness to it.

study.christ:
This passage points to Christ most clearly through the vision, and then through the single sentence in verse 5.

The Lord who appears to Paul at night is the risen Jesus. Luke does not say 'the Lord' means Jesus here, but the pattern of Acts is that the ascended Christ directs His servants, as in 9:5, 22:17-18, 23:11 and 27:23. Jesus says to Paul 'I am with you.' This is the promise with which He closed His earthly teaching, 'I am with you always, to the very end of the age,' Matthew 28:20, and the name Immanuel, God with us, Matthew 1:23. The presence He promised the church as it went out is delivered to one frightened man in one hard city.

He is the shepherd who counts the flock before it is gathered. The statement that He has many people in Corinth matches His own words, 'I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to My voice,' John 10:16. It also fits the Father's gift, 'All that the Father gives Me will come to Me,' John 6:37. Christ is the one who knows His people by name and sees them where the preacher sees only a pagan port. The apostle's task is to call them in.

He is the Christ whom Paul testifies to the Jews. Verse 5 says Paul testified that Jesus is the Christ, and that is the dividing line. To many in Israel, that is a stumbling block, and to the Greeks foolishness, but to those who are called it is the power and wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:22-24, which is how Paul describes his preaching in Corinth. He resolved to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and Him crucified, 1 Corinthians 2:2.

He is the one who gives rest to the weary servant. The Lord's night word gives permission to stay, and the staying lasts a year and a half, which shows how a single sentence from Christ can change the length of a mission.

To avoid forcing the text, some details have no direct Christ-reference. The tentmaking, the vow and the sea voyage are part of the story rather than pictures of Him. But Paul's tent-working life in service of others echoes the humility of the one who came not to be served but to serve, Mark 10:45.
study.god:
The Corinth passage shows a God who speaks to the afraid, governs courts and gathers His own.

He is a God who speaks. Luke does not leave Paul's discouragement unanswered. The Lord breaks into a night with specific words that match the need. The God of Scripture is not silent when His servants quail. He comes in the voice that fits, brief, personal and firm. The commands are short, and the reason follows each one.

He is present. 'I am with you' is the heart of what He is to His people, from Jacob at Bethel to the disciples on the mountain. The presence is not an extra comfort but the ground of obedience. Nobody could do what Paul did in Corinth without it.

He is protective, and the protection is specific. The promise that no one will lay a hand on him to harm him is carried out in the Gallio scene. But Scripture does not make God a guarantee against all suffering, since this same apostle later endures beatings and imprisonment. The promise fits the work: nobody could stop the work in Corinth until it was done.

He is the sovereign Lord of rulers. Gallio does not know he is serving God's purpose, and he would likely have been surprised to hear it, yet his refusal shields the church. Proverbs 21:1 says the king's heart is a stream of water in the Lord's hand. God uses a sceptical official, an angry crowd and a quarrel in a synagogue to carry out one plan.

He is a God who has a people before they know Him. 'I have many people in this city' is one of the most surprising lines of the book. It tells us that God's choice and love are not merely a response to our faith but go before it. Yet He gathers them through preaching, so His sovereignty does not cancel the missionary's task but secures its fruit.

He is also a God who invites worship and humility. 'If God is willing' is the way Paul speaks of every plan, and the way the church is taught to live. For worship, this means that we can rest in a promise and still hold our plans open to His will.

crossReferences.note: Paul tells the Corinthians that he came among them in weakness, fear and much trembling, and resolved to know nothing but Christ crucified. It is the inner story behind the night vision of Acts 18:9-10, and explains why the Lord's words, 'Do not be afraid,' were so well timed.

The Lord tells the young prophet not to be afraid of them, for He is with him to deliver him. Paul's vision uses the same two promises in the same order, fear banished by presence, and so places him in the line of the prophets sent to hard audiences.

After Elijah's complaint that he alone is left, the Lord reveals that He has kept seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal. Paul's discouragement meets the same answer, and Paul himself uses the story in Romans 11:2-5 to describe a remnant chosen by grace.

Jesus' closing promise, 'I am with you always,' spoken as He sent His disciples to all nations. The Lord's word to Paul in Corinth is the same promise personally applied. It shows that the Great Commission rests on the presence of the one who gives it.

The watchman who warns the people has delivered his own life, but the one who fails to warn is held accountable. Paul's declaration in Acts 18:6, 'Your blood be on your own heads,' draws on this picture, in which the messenger's task is faithful warning and the hearers answer for their response.

At Pisidian Antioch Paul and Barnabas first announce a turn to the Gentiles after opposition, citing Isaiah 49:6. The pattern repeats at Corinth, verse 6, and again at Rome, 28:28. Luke wants readers to see it as a rhythm and not a single break.

Paul reminds the Thessalonians that he worked night and day so as not to burden them while he preached. It is the same practice that Luke records in Corinth, verse 3, and shows that tentmaking was a settled policy for the sake of the gospel.

Paul says he baptised only a few of the Corinthians, including Crispus and Gaius. Crispus is the synagogue ruler of Acts 18:8, and the verses show that the people Luke names in one sentence were real members of the church to whom Paul later wrote.

Paul greets Priscilla and Aquila as his fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for his life, with a church in their house. It shows that the partnership begun over a workbench in Corinth became one of the lasting alliances in the early church.

The good shepherd knows His sheep and has others not of this fold whom He must bring. The Lord's statement in Acts 18:10 that He has many people in the city is this same shepherding knowledge, applied to a particular place.

Instead of boasting about plans, believers should say, 'If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.' Paul's remark at Ephesus, 'if God is willing,' in Acts 18:21 is a living example of the same humility.

study.oneStory:
Corinth shows what the promise to Abraham looks like when it reaches a port city. 'All the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' Genesis 12:3, now means a gathering of Greeks, Jews, slaves and merchants in the shadow of the temples of Corinth. The Lord's statement that He has many people in the city is the harvest of that promise in one place and one year. The group that meets next to the synagogue is one of the early signs that the family of Abraham is becoming multitudes from every nation.

The passage also echoes an older pattern about cities. In Genesis, cities begin with Cain and with Babel, humanity's attempt to make a name for itself. The Bible's story from there moves toward another city, the new Jerusalem, where God Himself dwells with people. Corinth, a city notorious for its vices, becomes the place where the Lord claims people for Himself, and later Paul can tell the church there, that some of them had once lived in just those ways but had been washed, sanctified and justified, 1 Corinthians 6:11. The story of redemption does not avoid the worst cities; it enters them.

It also shows the long answer to Israel's exile and scattering. The servant of Isaiah was to be a light to the nations, and the nations are now streaming in. Yet the story remains open to the Jews: Crispus the ruler of the synagogue believes, and Paul keeps going back to the synagogues, and Romans 11 holds out hope for all Israel.

And the passage shows how God brings His purpose through ordinary things: a workbench, a rented house next to a synagogue, a proconsul's indifference, a promise at night. It points forward to the end, when the Lord says again to His people, 'I am with you,' and the throne is surrounded by those redeemed from every tribe, language, people and nation, Revelation 5:9. The many people of Corinth are part of that crowd, and the words 'do not be afraid' are answered at last by a city where God lives among them and wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:3-4.

quiz.q: What did the Lord promise Paul in the night vision at Corinth?

options.text: His presence and protection, because He had many people in that city.
options.note: The Lord says do not fear, I am with you, and I have many people in this city.

options.text: That Paul would suffer no hardship for the rest of his life.
options.note: He promised protection in Corinth, but not a life free of all hardship; Paul suffered much elsewhere.

options.text: That the whole city of Corinth would be converted.
options.note: He promised many people, His chosen ones, not the conversion of the entire city.

options.text: That Paul should leave Corinth at once for his own safety.
options.note: The opposite: the Lord told him to keep speaking and not be silent, and he stayed a year and a half.

quiz.q: What does the Lord's word, I have many people in this city, teach about evangelism?

options.text: God's prior choice of a people fuels bold, persistent preaching rather than silencing it.
options.note: Election is given as the reason to keep speaking, so it grounds and motivates evangelism.

options.text: God already has His people, so preaching is what gathers them in.
options.note: True and close, but it slightly understates that the promise is given precisely to embolden Paul against fear.

options.text: Since God has chosen them, Paul's preaching made little difference.
options.note: This misreads election; God's choice is worked out through the means of Paul's preaching, not apart from it.

options.text: God saves people regardless of whether the gospel is preached.
options.note: The command to keep speaking shows the gospel is the means by which God's people are called.

quiz.q: How did Gallio respond to the charges against Paul?

options.text: He refused to judge what he saw as an internal Jewish dispute and drove them off.
options.note: Gallio dismissed the case as a matter of words, names, and their own law.

options.text: He found Paul innocent after hearing his defense.
options.note: Paul was effectively protected, but Gallio dismissed the case before Paul even spoke, rather than hearing a defense.

options.text: He handed Paul over to the synagogue for punishment.
options.note: He did the opposite, driving the accusers away from the judgment seat.

options.text: He condemned Paul and had him imprisoned.
options.note: Gallio refused the case; Paul was not condemned or imprisoned here.

quiz.q: How did Paul support himself while ministering in Corinth?

options.text: He worked as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla.
options.note: Luke notes he stayed and worked with them because they shared the tentmaking trade.

options.text: He labored with his own hands rather than burden the church.
options.note: True in substance, but the specific detail is that he worked at tentmaking with Aquila and Priscilla.

options.text: He was fully funded by the Jerusalem church.
options.note: There is no such funding here; he worked to support himself.

options.text: He collected fees from those he taught in the synagogue.
options.note: Paul refused such support in Corinth; he worked a trade instead.

quiz.q: What was the central claim of Paul's synagogue preaching in Corinth?

options.text: That Jesus is the Christ, the promised Messiah.
options.note: Luke says Paul testified to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ.

options.text: That salvation is now offered to the Gentiles.
options.note: He did turn to the Gentiles, but his testimony to the Jews centred on Jesus being the Christ.

options.text: That believers must keep the law of Moses.
options.note: That was the error rejected at the Jerusalem council, not Paul's message.

options.text: That Caesar was to be honored as lord.
options.note: Paul proclaimed Jesus as Christ, not Caesar as lord.

questions: The Lord told Paul, do not be afraid, keep on speaking. Where has fear made you fall silent, and how does Christ's promise of His presence steady you?
God had many people in Corinth who were not yet converted. How does knowing that God is already at work in people you have not reached change the way you pray and speak?
Paul worked a trade to support his ministry. How do you see your ordinary work as a place and means for serving Christ?
God restrained opposition through Gallio, a man who cared nothing for the gospel. Where might you trust God's providence over circumstances and authorities you cannot control?
Paul stayed a year and a half in a hard city because the Lord told him to. Where might faithfulness look like patient, unspectacular staying rather than moving on?

translationNotes.note: The reference to Claudius ordering the Jews to leave Rome fixes the setting around AD 49 and explains how Aquila and Priscilla came to Corinth. Footnote markers in the source were omitted when building the verse text.
The crowd renders literally they all; some manuscripts read all the Greeks. Either way, Sosthenes the synagogue leader is beaten while Gallio declines to intervene.

Some later manuscripts add that Paul intended to keep a feast in Jerusalem before returning; the earliest text simply has his promise to come back if God is willing, and this study follows that reading.
